message.content:
The sea had been Elias’s only companion for thirty years. Its voice was a constant, low growl against the granite cliffs, a rhythm he knew better than his own heartbeat. One grey morning, after a storm that had chewed the horizon, he found a bottle wedged in the rocks below the lighthouse. It was thick, green glass, sealed with wax.

Inside, a single sheet of paper, brittle as a dead leaf. The ink was faded, the handwriting a frantic scrawl: *“My dearest, if you find this, know I am still waiting. The tide is rising, but my love for you is higher. I am on the island with the crooked pine. Come before the moon wanes.”*

Elias read it three times. There was no name, no date. He knew every island within a hundred miles. There was no crooked pine. The message was a ghost, a whisper from a story that had already ended.

He should have thrown it back. Instead, he placed the bottle on his windowsill, next to the lamp. That night, as the great beam swept its arc of warning and welcome, Elias looked at the bottle. He thought of the desperate hope that had sealed it, the love that had outlasted the storm, the sender, and the shore.

He never found the island. But every night after, as he polished the lens and trimmed the wick, he felt a little less alone. The message wasn’t for him, but it had been found. And in the vast, lonely dark, that was enough.
